Memory Jogger.new: The SSA sued a disabled U.S. citizen to recover SSI payments made after he moved to Puerto Rico; the Court held 8--1 that the Fifth Amendment does not require Congress to extend SSI to Puerto Rico, because the territory's general exemption from federal income taxes supplies a rational basis under the Territory Clause (\href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/596/20-303/}{Justia}).

Judicial Votes.new: The Supreme Court \textbf{reversed} the First Circuit by an \textbf{8--1} vote. The case was argued on November 9, 2021, and decided on April 21, 2022 (\href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/596/20-303/}{Justia}; \href{https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/20-303}{Cornell LII}):

Analysis of Opinions.from: Joined the majority in full, but

Examples: Future Applications.new: \item \textbf{Same-Side (Territorial Exclusion Upheld): A Federal Heating and Cooling Credit.}

Examples: Future Applications.src: Congress enacts a new federal ``National Heating and Cooling Credit'' funded from general Treasury revenues and administered directly by the IRS, available to low-income households in the 50 States and D.C., but excluding residents of Guam and Puerto Rico while maintaining separate block grants for those territories. A disabled U.S. citizen living in Guam sues under the Fifth Amendment.

Congress wins under \emph{Vaello Madero}, \href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/435/1/}{\emph{Torres}}, and \href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/446/651/}{\emph{Rosario}}. Under the Territory Clause and deferential rational-basis review, Guam's distinct federal tax structure supplies a rational basis for territorial exclusion without any dollar-for-dollar accounting.

Examples: Future Applications.new: \item \textbf{Same-Side (Territorial Asymmetry Upheld): A Cap on Federal Medicaid Funds for the Territories.} Congress funds Medicaid in the States through an open-ended federal match but gives Puerto Rico and the other territories a fixed annual block of federal money, so that once the cap is reached the territory must pay the full cost. Low-income residents of Puerto Rico argue that the disparity denies them equal protection. Under \textit{Vaello Madero}, Congress may weigh the general balance of benefits to and burdens on territorial residents, including their exemption from most federal income taxes, the cost of greater reimbursement, and the risk of disrupting the territory's economy. \textit{Harris v.\ Rosario} upheld lower AFDC reimbursements to Puerto Rico on similar reasoning, and the cap survives rational-basis review.
\item \textbf{Opposite-Side (Exclusion Invalid): Excluding Residents of a State.} Now suppose Congress

Examples: Future Applications.src: excludes residents of West Virginia from the same federal credit because West Virginia residents pay less per capita in federal income taxes than residents of New York

Examples: Future Applications.new: . \textit{Vaello Madero}'s rationale does not carry over:

Examples: Future Applications.src: Congress cannot rely on the Territory Clause, and \emph{Vaello Madero} Footnote 1 expressly refuses to extend territorial fiscal-balance deference to exclusions of individual States---which would also collide with structural principles of equal state sovereignty and interstate travel.

Examples: Future Applications.new: \item \textbf{Opposite-Side (Strict Scrutiny): An Ancestry-Based Exclusion in Puerto Rico.} Alternatively, suppose Congress

Examples: Future Applications.src: excludes Puerto Rico residents from SSI only if they are of Hispanic ancestry while granting SSI to non-Hispanic residents of Puerto Rico

the classification ceases to be a geographic/territorial line and becomes an explicit racial or national-origin classification triggering strict scrutiny under Fifth Amendment equal protection (\href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/515/200/}{\emph{Adarand}}; or, on Justice Thomas's view, violating the Citizenship Clause), which the federal government cannot survive.

Examples: Future Applications.new: \item \textbf{Fence-Sitter (Close Call): Excluding Puerto Rico From a Payroll-Tax-Funded Benefit.} Congress creates a federal paid family-leave benefit financed entirely by a new payroll tax that is collected from workers and employers in Puerto Rico just as in the States, but it pays benefits only to residents of the States. A worker in Puerto Rico who paid the tax is denied benefits. \textit{Vaello Madero} rested on Puerto Rico's exemption from federal income taxes, a rationale that is missing when residents pay the very tax that funds the program, much as Justice Sotomayor stressed that Puerto Ricans pay payroll taxes. Yet rational-basis review accepts any conceivable justification and the majority looked to the general balance of benefits and burdens rather than any one tax, so a court could uphold the exclusion. The outcome is genuinely uncertain.
